title: Bridge the Gap — Healthy Cities
description: Air, water, waste and food taught as health in twenty-six Delhi-NCR schools, and ten Influence Fellows funded to pilot their own idea in eight states.
deck: What a city’s air, water, waste and food do to the health of the people in it — taught for a year in twenty-six Delhi-NCR schools, and piloted by ten funded fellows.
identity: Swechha is an environmental organisation in Delhi, working since 2000 — air, the Yamuna, schools, journeys and a five-acre farm.
partnership: In partnership with the Bupa Foundation and Niva Bupa Health Insurance

what.head: The city and the body
what.lead: The programme calls its subject the environment-health nexus: what a city’s air, water, waste, food and green cover do to the people breathing, drinking and eating in it. Children carry the worst of it and get taught the least about it.
what.line: A city gets into a child’s lungs long before it gets into their syllabus.

rows.p: Air pollution and respiratory health. Contaminated water and disease outbreaks. Urban food systems and nutrition. Waste infrastructure and health. Biodiversity and mental well-being. Those five links are the curriculum.

Schools were picked to bridge the gap between those most impacted by climate change and those with the power and agency to drive long-term solutions. Government schools have the ground and not the budget; private-school students have the consumption and the reach.
Children and youth must be the targets of change today to be the vehicles of change tomorrow.

A curriculum inside twenty-six Delhi-NCR schools, and the Influence Fellowship: a national open call that funded ten people to pilot their own environment-health solution where they already live and work.

kinds.lead: A curriculum, twenty trips out into the city, twenty gardens that have to survive a Delhi summer, and ten funded fellows.

workshops.head: Workshops
workshops.lead: A named curriculum — Bridge The Gap: Healthy Cities — delivered in five theme-based modules inside the school timetable rather than beside it.

rows.p: Air pollution and respiratory health. Contaminated water and disease outbreaks. Urban food systems and nutrition. Waste infrastructure and health. Biodiversity and mental well-being.
Inquiry-driven, experiential and solution-oriented: roleplays, expert interactions, simulations, classroom audits and action research tools. Not a lecture with a slide deck.
Each class identifies a locally relevant theme, and that theme becomes the anchor for its own green action project. The workshops are where the garden gets decided.
The year was set at twenty of each, and both were delivered.

prose: A school year is the unit that matters here. A single workshop is a morning. A year is long enough for a bed to be dug, planted, watered through a Delhi summer and replanted — and for the students who did it to be the ones explaining it to the next lot.

cityscapes.head: CityScapes
cityscapes.lead: Facilitated half-day visits out into the city the curriculum is about — twenty were set for the year and twenty ran — with the educators along rather than waiting at the gate.

rows.p: Forests, rivers, biodiversity parks and waste management sites. Forest and biodiversity walks, tree walks, and the Yamuna in Delhi — the only river Delhi has and the one most of these students had never stood beside.

rows.h: What a trip is made of
rows.p: Guided reflection sessions, stakeholder conversations and mapping activities. Students identify what natural heritage is there, what is happening to it, and what could be done about it.
Educators join the reflection, the conversations and the mapping. They are the ones who carry the subject through the rest of the year, so they are on the trip and not back at school.

prose: Seeing and believing, believing and learning, learning and doing. A drain is an idea until you are standing over it, and then it is a smell, a colour and somebody’s afternoon.

actions.head: Green action projects
actions.lead: Twenty gardens were set for the year and twenty got built, each one aligned to the theme that school’s own students picked in the workshops. Living, breathing classrooms rather than a plantation photograph.

rows.p: Food gardens, butterfly and pollinator gardens, green walls, spiral gardens, hydroponics units, AQI tree zones and clean air corridors, and composting units.
Butterfly gardens, composting units, a food forest patch, and an AQI tree zone or green wall. The hydroponics and the spiral gardens are in no plan — schools built them anyway.

rows.h: The garden is the health intervention
rows.p: Indigenous trees and shrubs — neem, peepal, arjun — for clean air corridors and shade. Kitchen and canteen waste into compost. Medicinal and fruit trees, herbs and vegetables in the schoolyard, for the air and for the food.
Conduct audits, mobilise peers, plan resources and monitor outcomes. The bed is the assignment, and it is marked in June.

prose: A plantation drive is a photograph. A garden is a rota. The difference between them is whether anybody is still turning up in June — so the bed sits inside the gate, a class owns it, and a teacher notices when it dies.

staff.head: The funder’s own staff, in a schoolyard
staff.lead: About forty Niva Bupa staff spent a day at MCD Pratibha Vidyalaya in Hari Nagar, designing and building gardens with fifty of the school’s students and the programme team.

rows.h: Three gardens, built on the day
rows.p: A small container food garden. A butterfly garden made out of old tyres. A vertical garden of indoor air-purifying plants. Three different answers to the same question, on one afternoon, on ground the school keeps.

rows.h: Staff and students on the same beds
rows.p: Forty people who fund the year and fifty who are taught by it, filling the same tyres and the same containers. The students designed alongside them rather than lining up for the photograph at the end.

rows.h: A day that left something standing
rows.p: A corporate volunteering day usually leaves a photograph. This one left three gardens inside a school gate, with a class that has to water them and a teacher who notices when they die — the same test every other garden on this page has to pass.

prose: Two hundred saplings went into the ground that afternoon.

statement.line: Twenty-six schools gave it a place in the year.

fellows.head: The Influence Fellowship
fellows.lead: A national open call, and nothing to do with the schools. Ninety-five people applied from across India for ten funded places; the ten who got them piloted an environment-health idea of their own, on the ground where they already live.

rows.p: Anyone residing in India, aged eighteen to thirty-five — students, early-career professionals, community leaders, social entrepreneurs and grassroots innovators, individually or as a team with one lead.
A grant of one lakh rupees, mentorship from environment and public health practitioners, implementation support, and certification as an Influence Fellow.
Clean air initiatives. Water conservation. Waste innovation. Sustainable food systems. Ecotherapy and nature-based wellbeing, which is mental health approached through ecology.
Ninety-five applications, scored on the idea, the feasibility and the person. The call opened in October and closed on ten names in November.

reach.head: Who else it reached
reach.lead: Two thousand students sat the workshops and took the trips.

rows.h: Twenty-six schools, a thousand to two thousand students each
rows.p: That is the multiplier, and it is the whole of the method. Each partner school has between one and two thousand children on its roll, so the schools that took this programme hold twenty-six to fifty-two thousand of them between them.

rows.h: Ten communities, five thousand people at the least
rows.p: The fellows were not visiting. Each of the ten worked where they already live, and the smallest of those communities holds more than five thousand people. Fifty thousand is the floor of what a soil school, a restored stepwell or a changed waste line was put in front of — it is not a headcount of who engaged with it.

figures.label: Students in the schools that ran it

rows.p: Three thousand saplings and seeds is the short-term number and the honest one: it is what went into the ground and got watered. The neem, peepal and arjun in those beds are trees in ten years, shade over a schoolyard that had none in fifteen, and after that a piece of the school’s own ground that nobody has to fund again.

rows.h: A bed now, an institution later
rows.p: A garden that survives a Delhi summer becomes a rota, and a rota becomes something the school runs without us: a compost line fed by its own canteen, a corridor of indigenous trees along the boundary wall, a plot the next class inherits with the assignment attached to it.
The programme’s own line is that children have to be the targets of change today to be the vehicles of it tomorrow.

voices.quote: Need of the hour and how else students will learn about managing their own waste.

The Varso Jal Sanchay Abhiyan provided meaningful experiential learning for our students by connecting heritage with water conservation. The visit to Valavav stepwell enhanced their understanding of traditional water systems and instilled a sense of responsibility towards protecting such structures. Initiatives like this are crucial for shaping environmentally conscious youth.
I had never really noticed the details of leaves before this workshop. Drawing them helped me slow down and observe things I usually ignore.

Participating in this project and Soil School activities helped me understand the importance of soil and sustainable agriculture. This experience motivated me to stay connected with agriculture and environmental work.

Being a part of this project for the first time made me realise that we as youth can bring about a change in our community. Not only by planting, but by also influencing others and spreading awareness.
